content: Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a parasitic disease caused by thread-like worms, primarily Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. These parasites reside in the lymphatic system, where they can live and reproduce for 4–6 years, releasing millions of microscopic larvae (microfilariae) into the bloodstream. The disease is transmitted between humans by mosquitoes. LF is endemic in 72 countries, with over 856 million people living in areas requiring mass drug administration (MDA) to prevent infection. The majority of cases are concentrated in India and parts of Africa, with smaller populations affected in Southeast Asia, the Pacific, and the Eastern Mediterranean. The Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF), launched by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2000, aims to stop the spread of LF through MDA and alleviate suffering by managing morbidity and preventing disability (MMDP). Since its inception, the program has delivered over 7 billion doses of antifilarial medicines, preventing an estimated 97 million cases of LF. However, despite these efforts, interventions to manage LF-related disabilities remain limited, with only 5% of known LF patients receiving MMDP care in endemic areas. LF manifests in both acute and chronic forms. Acute symptoms, often referred to as acute attacks or acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA), involve sudden swelling, redness, warmth, and pain in the affected area, often accompanied by fever, chills, and weakness. These episodes are typically caused by secondary bacterial infections entering through skin breaks, such as cuts or lesions between the toes. Chronic manifestations include lymphedema (or its advanced form, elephantiasis), hydrocele, and chyluria. Lymphedema, characterized by progressive swelling of the limbs, breasts, or genitals, can lead to thickened skin, folds, and mossy lesions, severely impairing daily activities. Hydrocele, a condition involving fluid accumulation in the scrotal sac, is a common LF-related complication in men. Management of LF-related morbidity focuses on preventing disease progression and improving quality of life. For lymphedema, this includes meticulous hygiene, skin care, and management of acute attacks with antibiotics. Advanced cases may require antifungal creams to prevent infections in deep skin folds. Hydrocele often necessitates surgical intervention. Community-based care programs, supported by health workers, play a critical role in ensuring patients maintain the best possible quality of life. The WHO has developed a comprehensive toolkit to assist national programs in planning, implementing, and monitoring MMDP activities. This includes clinical guidelines, operational strategies, and tools for evaluating program effectiveness. The second edition of the WHO’s manual on managing LF-related morbidity incorporates updated strategies and resources to expand access to essential care packages, particularly in endemic settings. It emphasizes the importance of integrating LF management with broader public health initiatives to achieve the 2030 targets for eliminating LF as a public health problem.
